lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
Date of birth: 3 Mar 1997 | Nationality: Canadian
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Cut the card-dispute form's abandonment rate from 37% to 22% in a four-week A/B test by splitting it into three short steps with saved progress.
- Ran 18 moderated usability sessions a quarter from a recruiting panel of 400 customers, so every major release was tested with real account holders before launch.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Raised the onboarding flow's System Usability Scale score from 68 to 104 across two rounds of moderated testing with 20 customers.
- Validated the redesigned app navigation's findability with an open card sort of 30 customers before it shipped.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Apr 2020 - Feb 2022
- Ran the monthly patient survey and rebuilt its reporting dashboard, cutting the time from survey close to published findings from 3 weeks to 4 days.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Wrote the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Championed an inclusive, human-centered design approach to transit wayfinding that delivered meaningful, user-first outcomes.
- Cut median route-finding time from 90 to 60 seconds, a 50% improvement, by adding audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA)
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interveiws, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality, personal details conventionally left off a résumé.
items.because: They are unrelated to qualifications and take space from relevant information.

items.says: Education appears before the established UX research experience.
items.because: The degree appears before the roles that demonstrate the candidate’s experience.

items.says: The timeline leaves 10 months unaccounted for between the degree and the first listed UX research role.
The release-coverage clause gives no research finding or decision resulting from the sessions.
items.because: The session cadence and panel show scope, but not how the research informed a release or improved the product.

items.says: The release-coverage clause is wordy and adds little beyond the sessions and customer panel.
The result is buried after several research sources and methods.
items.because: A scanning reader may move on before reaching the 23% reduction.

items.says: The reported SUS score of 104 exceeds the standard scale’s 100-point maximum.
items.because: Standard SUS scores range from 0 to 100.

items.says: “Moderated testing” is redundant after the line has stated the testing context.
An open card sort does not directly test findability in the redesigned navigation.
items.because: It shows how participants group and label content, not whether users can find items in a specific navigation design.

items.says: The card-sort claim gives no finding or design decision that resulted from the research.
items.because: The participant count shows the study’s reach, but not what changed or what the research demonstrated.

items.says: “Before it shipped” adds timing detail that does not clarify the card-sort result.
The strongest result comes after the research setup instead of opening the bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the research lead-in before the completed sign-up improvement.

items.says: The strongest result comes after the interview setup instead of opening the bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the interview count before the reduction in missed appointments.

items.says: The 30% reduction lacks a comparison period or baseline.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what the percentage is measured against.

items.says: The approach is described broadly rather than through a specific design action.
items.because: A reader cannot picture a concrete design decision or skill.

items.says: The claim of meaningful outcomes does not say what changed for users or provide evidence of the result.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what value the project created from the general claim.

items.says: The stated 50% improvement is wrong for the reduction from 90 to 60 seconds.
items.because: The time fell by 30 seconds from a 90-second baseline, a 33.3% reduction.

items.says: The stated 20% increase misstates the change from 65% to 85%.
items.because: It is an increase of 20 percentage points, or about 30.8% relative to 65%.

items.says: The repeated method uses space without describing a distinct contribution.
The redesign claim does not say what design change was made.
items.because: A reader cannot picture the UX decision behind the booking-step reduction and change in phone bookings.

items.says: The claim that the issues stopped first-time users generally from completing bookings overstates what the testing establishes.
items.because: Hallway testing with 10 patients does not establish that first-time users more broadly were prevented from completing bookings.

items.says: The line gives no resulting change in booking completion after the issues were fixed.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the fixes improved successful bookings or how much they helped.

items.says: The Skills, Methods line misspells “interviews.”
items.because: The visible typo may distract a reader and raise a question about attention to detail.
